questions.question: A loss has positive atoms, continuous subdensity $f_c$ and CDF $F$. Between the atoms, what component does the ordinary derivative $F'$ represent, with equality understood almost everywhere?
options: The whole probability law including its point masses.
Only the total weight of its discrete component.
The density conditional on being in the continuous component.
Only the continuous component density.

questions.question: A mixture selects one of two absolutely continuous loss laws with positive weights summing to one. Neither component has any point mass. Must the resulting law be mixed discrete and continuous?
options: No; averaging these laws creates no point masses.
Yes; two component laws create a discrete component index in the loss.
Yes; unequal component means force jumps in the loss CDF.
Yes; different density shapes give atoms where the curves cross.

questions.question: A proposed non-negative loss law has atom masses $p_1,p_2>0$ at two distinct amounts and a continuous subdensity $f_c\ge0$ with positive total area. Which normalisation condition accounts for all three pieces?
options: $\int_0^\infty f_c(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1$, with atoms added separately.
$p_1+p_2=1$, with continuous density added separately.
$p_1+p_2+\int_0^\infty f_c(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=1$.
$p_1+p_2+\int_0^\infty f_c(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=2$.

questions.question: A loss CDF $F$ has a jump at amount $a$, with $F(a-)=\mathbb{P}(X<a)$. Which formula isolates its atom mass for every such CDF and atom location, including when lower losses are possible?
A loss has $\mathbb{P}(X=a)=p>0$ at one fixed amount $a$. Could one ordinary integrable density with respect to interval length represent its entire probability law?
options: No; integration over the singleton cannot yield the positive mass.
Yes; assigning density height p at a supplies the atom.
Yes; spreading p over a narrow interval preserves the entire law.
Yes; using the density conditional on other losses supplies it.

questions.question: A loss equals zero with probability $0.8$ and otherwise is uniform on $(0,100)$. What is its unconditional continuous component density $f_c(x)$ for $0<x<100$?
A loss equals zero with probability0.8 and otherwise is uniform on(0,100). Its continuous subdensity at50 is0.002. What is the probability that the loss equals exactly50?
A loss has atoms at $a<b$ and CDF $F$, with $F(a-)=0.2$, $F(a)=0.4$ and $F(b)=0.9$. What is $\mathbb{P}(a\le X\le b)$?
A loss equals $10$ with probability $0.4$ and otherwise is uniform on $(0,10)$. What is its unconditional mean?
A loss equals zero with probability $1/2$ and otherwise is uniform on $(0,2)$. What is $\mathbb{E}[X^2]$, using both parts of the mixed law?

A loss law places weight $q$ at zero and weight $1-q$ on a uniform distribution on $(0,1)$, with $0\le q\le1$. For which weights does it have both a positive atom and a positive absolutely continuous component?

A loss has atom mass $p\in(0,1)$ at zero and positive continuous subdensity $f_c$ on $x>0$ of total area $1-p$. Which conditional density formula for $X>0$ is valid for every admissible $p$ and $f_c$?
options: $f_c(x)$ for $x>0$.
$f_c(x)/p$ for $x>0$.

questions.question: A mixed loss has a continuous subdensity $f_c$ and a separate positive atom at $a$. Only the finite value assigned to $f_c(a)$ is changed. What happens to the distribution?
options: The atom changes by the difference between density heights.
The continuous probability changes by that height difference.
It stays unchanged, including the separately specified atom.
The separate atom disappears when the new height is positive.

questions.question: A loss has atom mass $0.2$ at zero, atom mass $0.3$ at ten, and continuous subdensity $0.05$ on $(0,10)$, zero elsewhere. What is $\mathbb{P}(X=0\text{ or }5<X\le10)$?
A loss has atom mass $0.3$ at zero, atom mass $0.2$ at ten, and continuous subdensity $0.05$ on $(0,10)$, zero elsewhere. What is its CDF value $F(4)$?
A loss equals zero with unknown probability $p\in(0,1)$ and otherwise is uniform on $(0,8)$. Its CDF satisfies $F(4)=0.7$. What is the zero-atom probability $p$?
A non-negative loss has mass $1-q$ at zero and, with weight $q\in(0,1)$, a positive continuous component whose mean is infinite. Can adding the zero atom make the unconditional mean finite?
options: Yes; any zero atom bounds the unconditional mean by its weight.
No; positive weight on the infinite-mean part still gives infinite mean.
Yes; only the mean conditional on a positive loss is infinite.
No; the zero atom itself contributes an infinite term.

questions.question: A proposed loss model assigns all probability to $X=0$ and zero weight to a positive continuous component. Can the ordinary conditional-probability formula identify a law for $X$ given $X>0$?
options: Yes; the conditional law is the same point mass at zero.
Yes; the unused continuous component becomes the observed positive-loss law.
No; the conditioning event has probability zero.
Yes; normalising the zero subdensity gives a unique density.

questions.question: Loss A has mass $1/2$ at zero and subdensity $1/2$ on $(0,1)$. Loss B has mass $1/2$ at one and the same subdensity on $(0,1)$. What do their CDFs at $1/2$ show about recovering a mixed law from its continuous subdensity alone?
options: $F_A(1/2)=3/4$ and $F_B(1/2)=1/4$; atom location matters.
$F_A(1/2)=F_B(1/2)=1/4$; the subdensity determines both.
$F_A(1/2)=F_B(1/2)=3/4$; total atom weight determines both.
$F_A(1/2)=1/4$ and $F_B(1/2)=3/4$; higher atoms enter earlier.

questions.question: Loss A has probability $1/4$ at amount two and otherwise is uniform on $(1,3)$. Loss B has probability $3/4$ at two and otherwise the same uniform law. Both means equal two. Which additional comparison refutes identifying the mixed law from that mean?
options: $\mathbb{P}(A=2)=\mathbb{P}(B=2)=0$ because two is inside the uniform interval.
$\mathbb{P}(A=2)=\mathbb{P}(B=2)=1/2$ because both means are two.
$\mathbb{P}(A=2)=3/4$ and $\mathbb{P}(B=2)=1/4$ from the continuous weights.
$\mathbb{P}(A=2)=1/4$ differs from $\mathbb{P}(B=2)=3/4$.
